Trump Pushes Back on AI Industry Pleas
 
Plus, 10-year Treasury yields fade after touching 5% and oil prices keep climbing
 
By Heard on the Street Staff
 
 
BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI/AGENCE FRANCE-PRESSE/GETTY IMAGES
 

This is an edition of the Markets P.M. newsletter, a recap of the day’s most important markets moves, delivered after the closing bell. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

What Happened in Markets Today

 

President Trump pushed back on the need for new regulations linked to artificial intelligence, waving off industry executives’ warnings. Microsoft said it published a provisional code of conduct that it aims to apply when training new AI models. A top Chinese official said AI is the “core engine of a new round of technological revolution” and the main battleground of its rivalry with the U.S..

 

Cybersecurity stocks rallied amid the heightened attention on AI safety. CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks each climbed 14%, while Fortinet jumped 9%. Chip stocks fell, including Nvidia, which declined 3%. Corning, another beneficiary of the AI trade, dropped 14% and led S&P 500 decliners.

 

Oil prices climbed after Saudi Arabia shut down a pipeline that had served as a crucial outlet for crude amid the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude rose 1%, topping $105 per barrel, and is up nine of the last 11 sessions and almost 74% year-to-date.

 

The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield briefly broke above 5%, pushed by the oil surge and deepening investor concerns about inflation. The yield on the benchmark bond fell back to about 4.96%.

 

Major stock-market indexes fell modestly. The Nasdaq declined 0.6%, the S&P 500 dropped 0.5% and the Dow industrials slipped 0.3%.

One Big Story

 
 
DANIEL HEUER/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

A global bond market rout pushed the 10-year Treasury yield to 5% for the first time since 2023, but it doesn’t erase the value of fixed income in a diversified portfolio.

 

For those thinking of buying, the market ructions have made bond yields more attractive, financial advisers say. Still, money managers say they are struggling to get their clients to deploy cash into the bond market. Individual investors have been holding more than $3 trillion in money-market funds. Many investors also have high concentrations of their portfolios in stocks because of the long bull market.

 
 
 

What’s Coming Up

 

• The Federal Open Market Committee is scheduled to begin meeting Tuesday, with the interest-rate decision set to be announced Wednesday afternoon.

 

• Tuesday’s earnings calendar is light. Companies reporting quarterly results include Trip.com and Forgent Power Solutions.
